title: The cry of joy
hook: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal: whoever says it is blessed, true is the Timeless

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru is the Granth, and your line: guru maneyo granth. Where did you look for an answer? Today, the shout that often follows, and a look back at the week. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

If you've ever been near a gurdwara on a big day, or at a Sikh parade, you've heard it. One voice calls out: bole so nihaal! And a whole crowd answers, louder than seems possible: sat sri akaal! It can shake windows. It comes at the end of the Ardas, at weddings, at the start of a procession, sometimes from a single grandmother at the kitchen table when the news is good. It isn't a quiet prayer. It's a cry of joy, and it has a name: the jaikara.
screen: `ONE VOICE CALLS.` → `A WHOLE CROWD ANSWERS.` → `THE JAIKARA.`

segments.voice: Inside the word jaikara, some readers hear jai, victory or praise, the word in a cheer of triumph. It's a call and response. The first half, bole so nihaal: whoever says it will be nihaal. Nihaal is a lovely word: blessed, fulfilled, full to the brim with joy. The second half, sat sri akaal: true is the Timeless One. Sat is truth. Sri is a word of honor. Akaal is the one beyond time, the name Sikhs use for God who has no beginning and no death. Put it together: whoever says this is filled with joy, because the Timeless is true. Sikh tradition links the jaikara with Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa, and in Sikh history it was raised before battle, a way of reminding fighters that the outcome belonged to the Timeless. Today it's raised at every kind of moment. And the second half has a life of its own. Sat sri akaal is also an everyday greeting in Punjabi, hello and goodbye, with the truth of the Timeless folded inside. Now, the week we just finished. Day 631, the gurdwaras left behind, prayed for from across a border. Then honor of the humble: God as the strength of the weak. The petition, where the reason is named. Forgive our mistakes. The last line, rising spirits, good for all. The couplet, the Guru is the Granth. And now the jaikara, the shout that closes it. A week that walked from grief, through humility and honesty, out into joy.
screen: `JAI: VICTORY, PRAISE.` · `NIHAAL: FILLED WITH JOY.` · `SAT SRI AKAAL: TRUE IS THE TIMELESS.` · `THIS WEEK: GRIEF, HUMILITY, JOY.` · then, large: `SAT SRI AKAAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, clearly. Sit up. Take a full breath. If you're somewhere you can, say it out loud: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal. If you're on a bus, say it inside, but give it the same full voice in your head. Then sit with the echo. Notice what changed in your chest and shoulders. A jaikara isn't meant to be muttered. It's meant to lift. Stay with that lift, breathing, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Jaikara. The Sikh cry of joy: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal. Whoever says it is filled with joy; true is the Timeless One.
Your line: sat sri akaal. Today, greet one person with it, or with your warmest hello, and mean the truth inside the greeting. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: After the Ardas and at joyful or solemn moments, one person calls bole so nihaal and the congregation answers sat sri akaal; sat sri akaal is also an everyday Punjabi greeting.
